common_name: Nancy Lindsay Italian Arum (Heavily Marbled Historic Selection)

planting.note: Plant tubers in fall, 3-4 inches deep, in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.

directions: This long-grown English selection, named for the plantswoman and collector Nancy Lindsay, emerges from dormant tubers in early autumn with glossy, arrow-shaped leaves patterned in pale cream-gray along the veins and midrib, a marking distinct in texture and distribution from the more evenly frosted 'Marmoratum'. The foliage holds its pattern through the coldest months, giving reliable winter and early-spring interest in shaded borders, before dying back in late spring ahead of the greenish spathe flowers and the showy spikes of orange-red berries that follow in summer. Because seedlings vary in how heavily they are marked, divide and replant offset tubers in late summer while dormant to preserve this particular clone's patterning.

planting.note: Plant small tubers 2-3 inches deep in early fall in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade beneath deciduous trees.

directions: Found as a chance sport in an English garden and named for its discoverer, this winter aconite produces an extra ring of small, rounded inner segments inside the usual cup of golden-yellow petals, giving each flower a fuller, more layered look than the single-flowered species. It opens in late winter atop the same ferny collar of green bracts as ordinary Eranthis hyemalis and shares its liking for humus-rich soil and dappled shade beneath deciduous trees. Because the extra petals are a vegetative sport rather than a seed-stable trait, plants are propagated only by careful division of the tuber clumps once dormant, so established groups increase slowly and are best left undisturbed for several years between divisions.

common_name: Schwefelglanz Winter Aconite (Pale Sulfur-Yellow Sterile Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant tubers as fresh as possible in late summer to early fall, 2-3 inches deep, in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; soak dry tubers 24 hours before planting.

directions: Raised in the Netherlands from the same Eranthis hyemalis x E. cilicica cross that produced 'Guinea Gold', this hybrid instead carries pale, cool sulfur-yellow flowers rather than deep gold, giving it a softer presence in the late-winter border. Like its sibling it opens its cup-shaped blooms above a ruff of finely cut, bronze-tinted bracts in the last weeks of winter, flowering slightly later and lasting a bit longer than the straight species. As a sterile hybrid it sets no viable seed, so clumps increase only gradually by division of the tuber offsets, and are best left in place once sited beneath deciduous shrubs or trees. It combines well with early snowdrops and species crocus for one of the first color displays of the gardening year.

common_name: Virescens Green-Flowered Wood Anemone (Historic Viridescent Sport)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Virescens is a curious old sport in which the flower's white sepals are replaced by small green, leaf-like bracts.

directions: Plant thin, brittle rhizomes 2 inches deep, horizontally, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees. Virescens is one of the oldest recorded sports of the wood anemone, a plant in which the usual white, petal-like sepals have reverted to small, ruffled, leaf-green bracts, giving each flower the odd, tufted look of a miniature rosette rather than a conventional bloom. Collectors and anemone specialists prize it as a conversation piece and a window into the species' floral development rather than for showy color, and it is grown and divided exactly as the species form, spreading slowly by creeping rhizomes before going fully dormant by early summer. It associates well in a woodland collector's bed alongside the more conventionally colored named forms of wood anemone.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Bowles' Purple, named for English plantsman E. A. Bowles, bears flowers in a deeper violet-purple than the lavender-blue of 'Robinsoniana'.

directions: Plant thin, brittle rhizomes 2 inches deep, horizontally, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees. Named for the early-20th-century English plantsman E. A. Bowles, this selection bears flowers in a richer, more saturated violet-purple than the pale lavender-blue of the better-known 'Robinsoniana', with a silvery sheen on the sepal reverse that shows well against the dark woodland floor. It opens in early to mid spring, closing at night and in overcast weather like other wood anemones, and spreads gradually by creeping rhizomes to form a slowly thickening carpet in a favorable site. It pairs well with early daffodils and other spring ephemerals, then disappears completely by early summer as the rhizome goes dormant; once sited, it resents disturbance and is best left undisturbed indefinitely.
